title: Mr. Y & The Standards in Public Office Commission
text:
Decision
Mr. Y & The Standards in Public Office Commission
From
Office of the Information Commissioner (OIC)
Case number: OIC-200204-A0A0P6
Published on 6 July 2026
Background
Preliminary Matter
My Analysis
Decision
Right of Appeal
Whether SIPO was justified in refusing access to certain records relating to the applicant, under section 15(1)(a) of the Act, on the basis that relevant records do not exist or could not be found after it had taken all reasonable steps to identify and ascertain their whereabouts
6 July 2026
Background
On 3 December 2025, the applicant requested copies of any records held by SIPO that refer to him or to the release to him of documents relating to a named TD, which were the subject of a legal settlement between the TD and SIPO.
On 3 February 2026, as SIPO had not issued a decision within the statutory timeframe, the applicant requested an internal review of the deemed refusal.
On 10 February, SIPO informed the applicant that it had no record of his request having been made and asked him if he wished to proceed with the internal review or to avail of the opportunity to have an original decision made on his request. The applicant asked for the internal review to proceed.
On 3 March, SIPO refused the applicant’s request under section 15(1)(a) of the Act, saying that, following searches of folders and emails and consultation with relevant teams, its position was that no records exist that come within the scope of his request.
On 4 March, the applicant applied to this Office for a review of SIPO’s internal review request. In his application, he said that it was not tenable for SIPO to rely upon section 15(1)(a) as he is aware from an earlier similar request, made under GDPR, that records relating to the matter do exist. The applicant included a SIPO DSAR Schedule from 2024, which, according to him, is evidence of the existence of relevant records. He said that he believes that some of these records contain commentary about him and his work as a journalist.
I have now completed my review in accordance with section 22(2) of the FOI Act. During the course of this review, the Investigating Officer requested submissions from SIPO. While I do not intend to repeat in full either SIPO’s submissions or those made by the applicant at the time of his application, I can confirm that I have had regard to both for the purposes of this review. I have decided to conclude this review by way of a formal, binding decision.
Scope of Review
SIPO has refused the applicant’s request under section 15(1)(a) of the Act. As such, this review is concerned solely with whether SIPO was justified in refusing access to records relevant to the applicant’s request on the basis that no relevant records exist or can be found after all reasonable steps have been taken to ascertain their whereabouts.
Preliminary Matter
Before I address the substantive issues arising, I wish to make a preliminary comment.
It is important to note that a review by this Office is considered to be “de novo", which means that in this case, it is based on the circumstances and the law as they pertain at the time of the decision and is not confined to the basis upon which the FOI body reached its decision.
Analysis and Findings
Section 15(1)(a)
Section 15(1)(a) of the FOI Act provides for the refusal of a request where the records sought do not exist or cannot be found after all reasonable steps to ascertain their whereabouts have been taken. Our role in a case such as this is to review the decision of the FOI body and to decide whether that decision was justified. This means that I must have regard to the evidence available to the decision maker and the reasoning used by the decision maker in arriving at their decision and also must assess the adequacy of the searches conducted by the FOI body in looking for relevant records. The evidence in “search” cases generally consists of the steps actually taken to search for the records along with miscellaneous and other information about the record management practices of the FOI body, insofar as those practices relate to the records in question.
SIPO’s submissions
In its submissions to this Office, SIPO outlined the searches it had conducted for records relevant to the applicant’s request.
At the outset, it said that all electronic records held by SIPO, including records relating to FOI requests, were maintained on its Document Management System (DMS), which was its primary archive. However, it said that further to a cyber-attack on 11 December 2025 this DMS was no longer available to it and as such it was not possible for any searches to be carried out of this repository for records relevant to the applicant’s request. However, SIPO said that some residual folders, with incomplete records, were identified on its G:Drive.
SIPO said that, on 10 February 2025, the decision maker had asked the applicant to identify any FOI requests he had previously made relating to the TD as this would facilitate searches for records relevant to his current request. However, SIPO said that the applicant had declined to do so.
SIPO further said that the decision maker consulted with the Head of the SIPO Secretariat and the Head of the Complaints and Investigations Unit (CIU) to ascertain where on SIPO’s remaining drives any potential records relevant to the applicant’s request would most likely be found. It said that following such consultation it was determined that any possible records would be found among FOI records. In the absence of a DMS to search, the view was that any records would exist only in the residual and incomplete FOI folders on the SIPO G:Drive.
SIPO said that it first searched the incomplete FOI folders only for records linking the applicant to the TD, i.e. not for records that relate to the applicant alone. However, SIPO said that it subsequently searched the folders for records relating to the applicant. It said that all folders that were located subsequent to these searches were examined and have been saved in the 2026/05 folder. SIPO said that it also searched for records relating to the TD but that there were no results.
SIPO further said that, as the decision maker was aware that there were more FOI requests from the applicant than these searches had identified, he proceeded to examine the full FOI log and all FOIs submitted by the applicant in order to find any between 2021 and 2025 that concerned the TD, bearing in mind that the legal matter referred to by the applicant occurred in 2021/2022. SIPO provided details of these search results by year. For the years 2023 to 2025, the decision maker searched all notes in the FOI logs, which it said contained nothing concerning the applicant and the TD combined. For the year 2022, as there were no notes on the log, SIPO said the decision maker searched in each folder pertaining to the applicant, but this resulted in nothing being found that concerned both the TD and the applicant combined. Finally, SIPO said that, for the year 2021, there were no notes in the FOI log and that a search of all existing folders showed that there were none relating to the applicant. According to SIPO, the decision maker also searched any FOI records on his H: Drive that referred to the applicant to see if any pertained to the TD, but there were none. SIPO said that from these searches it appeared that no records pertaining to the TD and the applicant existed and that a refusal on administrative grounds was the only option available. SIPO said that it had concluded that any further records relating to an FOI request by the applicant with respect to the relevant TD were now no longer available.
In addition, SIPO noted the applicant’s reference to the DSAR folder in his application to this Office. It said that this information would have been very useful at the time of the original request but that it was not provided. SIPO said that, in the absence of a cross-referenced DMS archive, there is no effective way to locate records other than to find folders where relevant records might exist and then to examine the content of these folders. SIPO said that, with this new information, CIU was able to find a DSAR folder on the SIPO G:Drive. SIPO said that, in this folder, it located a number of records connected to the applicant, including records relating to a previous FOI request, an email chain between the applicant and a SIPO staff member in which the applicant made enquiries and received answers, and two copies of a newspaper article on the TD written by the applicant. SIPO noted that the applicant will already be in possession of these records. According to SIPO, neither a DSAR decision letter nor a DSAR schedule of records were found in the DSAR folder.
SIPO went on to say that its normal practice was to retain FOI files on the DMS. SIPO also said that the applicant may be correct in saying that relevant records existed in 2024 but added that all DSAR requests and records were held on the DMS, which is no longer accessible and cannot be searched.
The Investigating Officer subsequently shared the DSAR schedule with SIPO, with a view to assisting more targeted searches. SIPO noted that the DSAR schedule details six released records and 45 legal advice records that were not released. SIPO said that it had compared the schedule with the contents of the G:Drive folder. According to SIPO, there is no similar grouping of records in the G:Drive folder but it acknowledged that there may have been a folder on the DMS containing the records. SIPO went on to say that it considered it most likely that the six released records listed on the schedule were those that it found on its G:Drive. With respect to the 45 legal advice records listed in the DSAR schedule, SIPO noted that the G:Drive folder contains a very large number of legal advice records. SIPO reiterated that it searched this folder and all sub-folders but could find no records that contain commentary about the applicant and his work as a journalist as referenced in the title of the record. SIPO said that the 45 legal advice records may have been compiled in a separate folder on the DMS. SIPO concluded that, in order to see if there may be a reference to the applicant in any of the legal advice records (the titles of which do not refer to him), however tenuous that possibility, it would be necessary to read through all the records in the DSAR folder.
The Investigating Officer subsequently sought further information from SIPO with respect to the records and the searches carried out. In its response, SIPO explained that the applicant’s relationship to the case of the TD was peripheral at best and it surmised that the legal advice records mentioned in its submission may have been included in the applicant’s DSAR folder purely because his newspaper article and the email chain were there.
SIPO went on to say that there were a total of 150 legal advice records relating to the case in a folder labelled ‘SIPO Legal Advice Library [TD’s initials]” and that these relate entirely to the legal process. SIPO explained that this was in addition to 102 records located in the other folders. SIPO said that it had searched the folders and examined all the titles of each of the records, reiterating that the only references to the applicant were as it had already detailed. SIPO added that, if it is necessary to search within each record using a keyword search, then this could be done but that it would take some time. SIPO reiterated that the records on the G: Drive are, at best, residual and incomplete and that this applies to the DSAR request records and the schedule that were prepared by the Data Protection Officer (DPO) at the time.
Finally, the SIPO decision maker said that he had discussed the matter with the current DPO and requested that she search for a possible DSAR folder on the G: Drive containing records that would respond to the DSAR Schedule. The decision maker added that, although such a folder is likely to have been saved on the DMS as the primary archive, there may be a residual folder that would help with this search process.
My Analysis
It is important to note that the FOI Act does not require absolute certainty as to the existence or location of records, as situations can arise where records are lost or simply cannot be found. What the FOI Act requires is that the public body concerned takes all reasonable steps to locate relevant records.
The question I must consider, therefore, is whether SIPO has taken all reasonable steps to ascertain the whereabouts of the specific records sought.
At the outset, I note that it is clear that further to the cyberattack of 11 December 2025, SIPO no longer has access to its primary electronic archive; the DMS. While this is unfortunate, it means that any searches for records relevant to the applicant’s request will necessarily be confined to what is termed the G:Drive which is acknowledged by SIPO to be residual and incomplete.
In the circumstances of the case, I am satisfied that the key issue which I must consider is whether SIPO has conducted all reasonable searches of the G:Drive for records relevant to the applicant’s request.
Having regard to the information before this Office, I am not satisfied that SIPO has taken all reasonable steps to locate the records sought by the applicant. It is evident from SIPO’s submissions that its searches to-date have located relevant records and, while it maintains that these are in the applicant’s possession, it does not appear to have verified this with the applicant. In addition, while I appreciate that searches have been complicated by the loss of the DMS and that the repository of records on the G: Drive appears to be residual and incomplete, SIPO’s submissions indicate that further searches could be conducted with a view to confirming whether relevant records still exist. While SIPO has indicated that these searches may take some time, I do not believe that the number of records involved would make such searches unreasonable.
Accordingly, having regard to the information before this Office, I simply cannot find that SIPO has taken all reasonable steps to locate further records sought by the applicant. In the circumstances, I find that SIPO was therefore not justified in refusing access to further records, under section 15(1)(a) of the FOI Act, on the grounds that no further records exist or can be found after all reasonable steps to ascertain their whereabouts have been taken.
Decision
Having carried out a review under section 22(2) of the FOI Act, I hereby annul SIPO’s decision. I find that SIPO was not justified in refusing access under section 15(1)(a) of the FOI Act to further relevant records coming within the scope of the applicant’s request and I direct it to make a fresh decision on the applicant’s FOI request.
Right of Appeal
Section 24 of the FOI Act sets out detailed provisions for an appeal to the High Court by a party to a review, or any other person affected by the decision. In summary, such an appeal, normally on a point of law, must be initiated not later than four weeks after notice of the decision was given to the person bringing the appeal.
